rashi:a1.1: To disqualify where there are brothers: if there are fit brothers with him and he went and performed ḥalitza with her, according to Rabbi Yehuda he has done nothing at all and has not disqualified her from the brothers; if one of the brothers wishes to take her in levirate marriage, he may. According to Rabbi Yosei, who treats him as an uncertainty, he has disqualified her from the brothers, since perhaps his ḥalitza is a valid ḥalitza, and none of the brothers can take her in levirate marriage, for once he did not build [his brother’s house], he may not build it again. Rather, they perform ḥalitza with her again.
rashi:a2.1: And to perform ḥalitza where there are no brothers: if there are no brothers but the tumtum, according to Rabbi Yehuda she is released with nothing at all, since he is certainly a eunuch and is as if he did not exist. According to Rabbi Yosei she requires ḥalitza, since perhaps he is not a eunuch; and when he said “he does not perform ḥalitza,” he said it of a case where there are brothers.
rashi:a3.1: We will return to you, Al Elu Mumin [the end of chapter 6].
rashi:a4.1: Mishna. These blemishes: those stated regarding the firstborn disqualify a priest from the service.
rashi:a4.2: Whether permanent or transient: for as long as they are on him.
rashi:a4.3: The kilon, the lifta and the makkavan: explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a4.4: And one whose head is shakut, and the sekifat: explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a5.1: And those with humps: this is a dispute; but those others, the kilon, the lifta and all of them, are agreed by everyone.
rashi:a5.2: Ḥatarot [humps]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)
rashi:a6.1: Gemara. Why: are they disqualifying in a person?
rashi:a6.2: But there is a wart: which is not written regarding a person.
rashi:a6.3: And furthermore, cataract and tevallul: which we stated among the blemishes of the firstborn, yet they are not written regarding an animal. Granted, all the others we listed for it, such as the gums and a calf’s tail that does not reach the leg joint, come from “any ill blemish.” But cataract and tevallul can be challenged: since the Merciful One revealed them for a person and did not reveal them for an animal, learn from this that they do not disqualify in an animal. And he answers: they are derived from one another.
rashi:a9.1: Garav, which is repulsive: more than yalefet, since it is hard as earthenware, sinks into the flesh and makes cracks.
rashi:a10.1: And let the Merciful One write them all: the blemishes, either for a person or for an animal.
rashi:a10.2: And garav and yalefet here and here: garav for the verbal analogy, and yalefet to show that garav is free. [Otherwise,] why did He write blind, lame and broken both here and here?
rashi:a11.1: Regarding which should He write: in which of them should the Merciful One write them, so that the other is derived from it?
rashi:a11.2: Closed hooves and gums, which do not exist in a person: for a person does not have parted hooves, and blemishes of the gums do not apply to him, since a person has teeth and the gums are not visible; whereas an animal has teeth above [so the printed text reads; cattle in fact have no upper front teeth, which is why the upper gum shows], and the gums are visible, and it is disqualified when they are damaged.
rashi:a11.3: In an animal too they should not disqualify: this is why the Merciful One wrote blemishes for an animal, and counted among them closed hooves and gums that were damaged or worn down, which come from “cracked” [ḥarutz].
rashi:a12.1: Gibben and ḥarum do not exist in an animal: a gibben is one who has [unusual] eyebrows [gevinim], called in Old French sourcils, and an animal has no eyebrows. A ḥarum is one whose nose [is sunken] between his two eyes, and an animal has no nose between the eyes.
rashi:a13.1: And those that do not exist in the other: that are not relevant to it, let Him write them in the other.
rashi:a14.1: That was introduced in it: and here there is something new in a person, gibben and ḥarum, and in an animal, closed hooves and gums.
rashi:a15.1: Why do I need: to write that blemishes disqualify in a person, and that blemishes disqualify in a firstborn, as it is written, “And if there be any blemish therein” (Deuteronomy 15:21), and that blemishes disqualify in consecrated animals?
rashi:a16.1: A person cannot be derived from a firstborn: that is, had He written it of a firstborn and not of these, a person could not be derived from a firstborn: what of a firstborn? It is fitting that a blemish disqualifies it, since it itself is offered.
rashi:a18.1: A person cannot be derived from consecrated animals: that is, had He written it of consecrated animals and not of these, these could not be derived from them.
rashi:a19.1: Their sanctity is great: [consecrated animals, with their many kinds:] sin offerings and guilt offerings, burnt offerings and peace offerings; a person, whose sanctity is great in commandments.
rashi:a22.1: A man who is equal among the seed of Aaron: it is he who needs a blemish [to be disqualified]; but one who is not equal among the seed of Aaron is disqualified even without a blemish.
rashi:b1.1: What is there: between a priest disqualified by a full blemish and a priest disqualified because he is not equal among the seed of Aaron, that is, the kilon, the lifta and all those.
rashi:b2.1: Because of appearance: such as those the mishna lists “because of appearance,” who are unpleasant to look at, such as one whose eyelashes fell out and one whose teeth were removed.
rashi:b2.2: A positive commandment: one who is not equal among the seed of Aaron transgresses a positive commandment if he served, for this is the implication: one who is equal among the seed of Aaron is a priest and shall serve; one who is not equal shall not serve. And a prohibition that comes by implication from a positive commandment has the status of a positive commandment.
rashi:b3.1: Like a cover [akhla]: like the cover of a barrel, which is narrow above and wide below. Its parallel is in Sanhedrin, chapter Zeh Borer (28b): “like a cover for a barrel.”
rashi:b3.2: Like the top of a turnip: the head of the turnip, which is wide and narrows as it goes down.
rashi:b3.3: In the middle of the head: his head protrudes behind as much as in front.
rashi:b4.1: Like a makkava: like an axe, whose back is rounded and short in width.
rashi:b4.2: Shakut in front: his head slopes diagonally in front, like a carpenter’s tool (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b4.3: Behind: the height of his head is lacking at the back.
rashi:b4.4: Shakil pisa: he looks like one from whom a piece has been taken.
rashi:b4.5: Ḥavi miḥba [hidden]: his head rests between his shoulders, and he looks like one whose head has sunk down (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). [Rashi’s text reads ḥavi miḥba, “hidden,” as the Davidson English translates; the printed Gemara reads ḥavis miḥbas, “pressed in.”]
rashi:b6.1: They taught only where he does not have: a row of hair encircling from ear to ear at the back, but has one in front.
rashi:b6.2: But if he has it at the back and in front he is fit, and all the more so if he has it at the back and not in front: since it is more becoming when he has it at the back and not in front than when he has it all around the head and is bald in the middle.
rashi:b7.1: And some teach it on the latter clause: the mishna’s “if he has, he is fit” was taught only where he has a row encircling from ear to ear at the back and not in front; but if he has one in front as well, he is disqualified, and all the more so if he has none at all.
rashi:b8.1: Zavlegan: whose eyes run and drip water.
rashi:b8.2: Dwarves, we learned: in the mishna (45b): “the kipe’aḥ, the dwarves and the deaf.”
rashi:b9.1: It was necessary for him [to teach] the zavlegan: which we did not learn [in a mishna].
rashi:b9.2: And lest you say, etc.: that is, these too were necessary. For lest you say that the mishna disqualifies them because of appearance, and they do not transgress a positive commandment if they serve, Rabbi Yoḥanan teaches us that it is because he is not equal among the seed of Aaron.
rashi:b10.1: The eyelashes: the hairs at the eye.
rashi:b10.2: And the same applies to all of them: from those with humps onward. For one might think that what we derived above from “one who is not equal among the seed of Aaron” refers only to the kilon, the lifta, the makkavan and those of the first clause.
rashi:b11.1: But wherever there is another case of “because of appearance,” he repeats it, as he teaches in the latter clause, “and one whose teeth were removed…”: from that I know that in the first clause, where he taught “appearance,” it refers only to one whose eyelashes fell out; for if it referred to all of them, why would he need to repeat it? So why did Rabbi Yoḥanan come [to teach this]?
rashi:b11.2: He came to exclude this tanna: who disqualifies them only because of appearance. Rabbi Yoḥanan teaches us that the halakha follows the mishna, which disqualifies them because they are not equal among the seed of Aaron.
rashi:b12.1: The priests: “And Aaron’s sons, the priests, shall lay…” (Leviticus 1:8).
rashi:b12.2: To include the bald: that they are fit for the service. I found it on this verse in Torat Kohanim.
rashi:b13.1: Mishna. Eyebrows [gevinim]: in Old French, sourcils.
rashi:b13.2: Whose eyebrows lie: the hairs of his eyebrows are long and lie over his face.
rashi:b14.1: Gemara. Many eyebrows: his two eyebrows join, with no smooth space between one and the other.
rashi:b14.2: This is the exposition of “or a gibben”: this is what it means: this is the “or a gibben” stated in the Torah (Leviticus 21). And Rabbi Dosa disagrees with him and does not expound “or.”
rashi:b15.1: That is to say it lives: one who has two backs and two spines, whom Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus disqualifies.
rashi:b15.2: It is not an offspring: and she does not have the impurity of childbirth.
rashi:b15.3: Prohibited for consumption: like a carcass, since it is a nonviable birth and is considered dead, and slaughter does not help it.
rashi:b16.1: Already raised it to him: in Tractate Niddah.
rashi:b16.2: Are you Shimi?: does a great scholar like you not know how to resolve the mishna? The mishna implies that he lives, so it does not mean literally two backs, but one whose spine is crooked and looks like many backs and spines; and when I spoke, I meant literally two backs.
rashi:b17.1: Mishna. One who paints both of his eyes as one: he has no nose at all between his two eyes, so when he paints his eyes with the kohl stick he can draw the stick from eye to eye, and the nose does not stop it.
rashi:b17.2: Both of his eyes above: as explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b17.3: Sekhei shemesh: who cannot look toward the sun.
rashi:b17.4: The zagdan and the tzairan: explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b17.5: His eyelashes: the hairs at the eye.
rashi:b17.6: Because of appearance: this refers to one whose eyelashes fell out.
rashi:b18.1: Gemara. Sunk: above, between his eyes.
rashi:b18.2: Soled [retreats]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss) short in length.
rashi:b18.3: Bolem [blocked]: its nostrils are stopped up.
rashi:b18.4: Notef [drooping]: long, and hanging down below his lip.
rashi:b18.5: You have gone too far: you have said too much; even if it is not sunken so much, he is a ḥarum.
tosafot:a6.1: In brief: The Gemara could equally have challenged from “cracked” [ḥarutz], which is not written of a person even though it applies to a person, in the gums and in the place of a bone, as in an animal. Likewise “crushed” and “cut” are not written of a person, and gibben is not written of an animal, even though it would apply to an animal according to the view below that a gibben is one whose spine is crooked, not one with unusual eyebrows. Tosafot then raise “no testicles, or only one,” which the mishna above (40a) counts as a blemish in an animal: that comes only from meroaḥ ashekh, as the first tanna later in this chapter calls it “the meroaḥ ashekh stated in the Torah,” and an animal is learned from a person by the verbal analogy just below. That works for the first tanna. But Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva need the verse for a missing testicle; from where do they know [the other case], which they themselves count as a blemish in the earlier chapter? If from “a visible blemish that does not return,” why would the first tanna need a verse for it? And they too would read the verse that way, were it not needed for the missing testicle. One cannot distinguish between a person and an animal on the grounds that an animal has two sacs, so the loss counts as more of a blemish, since even “no testicles at all” must be excluded from meroaḥ ashekh. Perhaps in such a case one may say that it was repeated for the new element it introduces, as the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches below; and this also explains why some blemishes are written even though they would follow from “a visible blemish that does not return.” Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a9.1: Garav, which the Merciful One wrote, why do I need it? [It is free]: This is puzzling, since it is needed for what Rava said in the previous chapter (41a): the Merciful One wrote garav to teach that a crack in the place of flesh is not a blemish. However, two garavs and two yalefets are written, one for a person and one for an animal, so one is left over to make it free. But then it is necessarily free on one side only, and there is an opinion in Bava Kamma (25b) that such an analogy can be refuted. Furthermore, since the baraita says, “The verse states: ‘scabbed’ and ‘scabbed,’ ‘scurvy’ and ‘scurvy,’” why does it need to draw the verbal analogy from both? This implies that it says so because in both places garav is written together with yalefet, to make it free. One may answer that Rava’s exposition above does not remove the freeing from here, since according to that exposition garav is not used for itself but only to teach about a crack [the printed text reads ḥarum, apparently for ḥarutz] in the place of flesh.
tosafot:a12.1: Gibben and ḥarum, which do not exist in an animal: this is according to the first tanna below in this chapter, who explains gibben as about the eyebrows. But according to Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus, who says he has two backs and two spines, it applies well to an animal. And that is why it does not also list meroaḥ ashekh [among those that do not exist in an animal], which according to Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus, who says it is anyone whose appearance is darkened, does not exist [in an animal]: because the Gemara here is not speaking according to him.
tosafot:a15.1: Why do I need that the Merciful One wrote a blemish in a person, a blemish in a firstborn, a blemish in consecrated animals? They are necessary, etc.: This is puzzling. Since it says “they are necessary,” which implies that we do not derive them from one another, from where do we know, for a person and for consecrated animals, every visible blemish that does not return, which for a firstborn we expound above in chapter Al Elu Mumin (37a) from a general rule and a detail? And likewise the blemishes of a person and of consecrated animals that are not written for a firstborn, some of which do not come from “any ill blemish,” such as cataract and tevallul, as Rashi explained at the beginning of this chapter. One may answer: since [the Torah] has revealed [that a blemish disqualifies in each case], it has revealed [that they share the same blemishes].
tosafot:b6.1: Rava said: they taught only, etc.: there is another reading in the books besides the reading of the Kuntres [Rashi].
tosafot:b15.1: In an animal it is prohibited for consumption: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained that slaughter does not help it because it is a nonviable birth, which implies that it speaks of one that came out into the air of the world. That cannot be said, since in chapter HaMappelet (Niddah 24a) it is set where it was found inside its mother, and Rav does not permit it through its mother’s slaughter, while Shmuel disagrees there and permits it through its mother’s slaughter; but if it came out into the air, it is prohibited even according to Shmuel. Rav Shimi raises his difficulty there from our mishna here, and there the Kuntres explained that he challenges both Rav and Shmuel, since this teaching of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus is taught among the blemishes of animals and disqualifies it for the altar, implying it is permitted for ordinary eating. Rabbeinu Tam challenged him, since here it is explicitly taught among the blemishes of a person. Rather, he challenges Rav alone, who says that in a woman it is not an offspring, so evidently it does not live; and since here it is disqualified from the service, evidently it lives. And so too the passage implies that he challenges only Rav.
tosafot:b17.1: Sekhei shemesh: the Gemara explains it as sanei shemesh, as the Kuntres [Rashi] explained: one who hates the sun and cannot look at a place where the sun shines. And sekhei means ḥasukhei shemesh, those from whom the sunlight is withheld.
tosafot:b17.2: And one whose eyelashes fell out: this implies that it calls ris the hairs, which tend to fall out from much weeping, as in the story of Rabban Gamliel in Ḥelek (Sanhedrin 104b) on “she weeps sorely.” And sometimes it calls ris the skin surrounding the eye, as in the previous chapter (38a), “a ris that was pierced or split,” explained there as the outer rim of the eye.
gershom:a1.1: These blemishes: which we count for an animal.
gershom:a2.1: Whether permanent or transient, they disqualify in a person: in priests.
gershom:a3.1: And in addition to them: which disqualify in a person and not in an animal: the kilon, etc.
gershom:a4.1: And why: do they disqualify in a person? But there is the wart, which is not written regarding a person and is written regarding an animal; and cataract and tevallul, which are not written in the Torah among the blemishes of an animal, so why does he count them here for an animal?
gershom:a5.1: They are derived from one another: the blemishes of an animal from the blemishes of a person; therefore he counts all of them for an animal.
gershom:a6.1: Garav and yalefet are written both among the blemishes of a person and among the blemishes of an animal, for the verbal analogy.
gershom:a7.1: And if yalefet, which is not repulsive: since it is dry.
gershom:a8.1: Garav, which is repulsive: since it is moist.
gershom:a9.1: And let the Merciful One write all the blemishes, the wart as well as cataract and tevallul, in one and not in the other, and only garav and yalefet in the other, to derive [the rest], either regarding a person or regarding an animal.
gershom:a10.1: Closed hooves and gums, which do not exist in a person: since a person’s gums are not exposed like an animal’s, they do not disqualify in a person; nor closed hooves, since we do not require split hooves in a person.
gershom:a11.1: Gibben and ḥarum, which do not exist in an animal: for a gibben is one whose eyebrows lie [over his eyes], and an animal has no eyebrows.
gershom:a12.1: And ḥarum: this is one who paints both of his eyes as one, since his nose is sunken and he has no nose between eye and eye, so he can paint from one to the other, with no nose between the eyes to stop it. And an animal has no such nose and does not paint its eyes.
gershom:a13.1: And let Him write all the blemishes that apply to one: if to a person, let Him write there gibben and ḥarum and all the blemishes.
gershom:a14.1: And those that do not exist in it, such as closed hooves and gums, let Him write in the other, the animal, and not write there any more of the blemishes except garav and yalefet; and let all the blemishes that apply to each one be derived from one another.
gershom:a15.1: Rather: they were written twice because of the new element in them; since one has what the other does not, He wrote them twice.
gershom:a16.1: A person, a priest, since he was included in many commandments, which is not so of a firstborn or of consecrated animals.
gershom:a17.1: Since their sanctity is greater: for consecrated animals apply to males and females alike, and furthermore they have many sanctities: sin offering and guilt offering, burnt offering and peace offering.
gershom:a18.1: Let Him not write it of a person, and let it come from these, from a firstborn and from consecrated animals. And if you say: what of a firstborn, whose sanctity is from the womb, will you say so of a person? Consecrated animals prove it, for they are not sacred from the womb and even so a blemish disqualifies them. What of consecrated animals, whose sanctity is great? A firstborn proves it. And the argument comes back around: the feature common to them is that a blemish disqualifies them, so too a person. [The answer:] what of these, which are offered upon the altar, which is not so of a person?
gershom:a19.1: What of these, consecrated animals and a person, whose sanctity is great: a person was included in commandments, and consecrated animals, since their sanctity is great. And the sanctity of a person, a priest, and of consecrated animals applies to ordinary ones and firstborn alike, being fit for the service.
gershom:a20.1: Their sanctity is automatic: they need not be consecrated.
gershom:a21.1: In addition to them in a person, the kilon, etc.: these are not disqualified by Torah law [as blemishes], but because we require a man who is equal among the seed of Aaron.
gershom:b1.1: What is there between one who is not equal among his seed and “because of appearance”: for “because of appearance” is more lenient than all of them.
gershom:b2.1: There is a positive commandment between them: as it is written, “of the seed of Aaron the priest”: one who is equal among the seed of Aaron is fit for the service, and one who is not equal is not fit; and this is a prohibition that comes by implication from a positive commandment, which has the status of a positive commandment. For “appearance” there is not even the prohibition of a positive commandment.
gershom:b3.1: The kilon: like the lid of a barrel, which slopes and is narrow at the top.
gershom:b4.1: Lifta: his head resembles a turnip, which is wide at the top on all sides.
gershom:b5.1: And it was taught: for example, his neck stands in the middle of his head, so that the head protrudes on all sides. Makkava: his head resembles a hammer, for the forehead protrudes far forward, and likewise the nape behind, while at the temples his head is even; it resembles a hammer that projects in front and behind. This is makkava, as in “and she took the hammer [makkevet] in her hand” (Judges 4:21).
gershom:b6.1: Shakut in front: his head protrudes greatly in front.
gershom:b7.1: And sekifa behind: he looks like one from whom a piece was cut at the back; and this is shakil pisa.
gershom:b8.1: Ḥavis miḥbas [pressed in]: his neck is sunk between his shoulders. And shamut [drawn out]: his neck is long and thin, and his face juts far forward.
gershom:b9.1: Those with humps: which they call in the vernacular (Rabbeinu Gershom adds a vernacular gloss).
gershom:b10.1: A piece of flesh [karkura]: this is merely a lump.
gershom:b11.1: And the zavlegan: some say he has rheum in his eye, and some say a discharge comes out of it.
gershom:b12.1: The bald and the dwarves we learned in the mishna, so what does he teach us? Let him teach us the zavlegan alone.
gershom:b13.1: He needed all of them, for lest you say they are disqualified because of appearance, he teaches us that it is because he is not equal among the seed of Aaron.
gershom:b14.1: And why would we be uncertain whether it is because of appearance? [The tanna states that reason wherever it applies.]
gershom:b15.1: Lest you say: he taught one case “because of appearance,” and the same applies to all of them; therefore Rabbi Yoḥanan teaches us that it is because he is not equal.
gershom:b16.1: And how can he say “he taught one and the same applies to all,” when wherever he can repeat and teach “because of appearance,” he repeats and teaches it? This shows that we do not say “he taught one and the same applies to all.” So what does Rabbi Yoḥanan teach us?
gershom:b17.1: Rather, this is what he teaches us: to exclude this tanna, etc.
gershom:b18.1: The priests: “and Aaron’s sons shall offer”; why then is “the priests” written? To include the bald.
gershom:b20.1: Anyone whose eyebrows lie: which are large and hang over his eyes.
gershom:b21.1: Rava said: “This is the gibben stated in the Torah” means: this is the exposition of “or a gibben” stated in the Torah; that is, from “or” it includes one who has only one eyebrow.
gershom:b22.1: In a woman it is not an offspring: since it does not live.
gershom:b23.1: Where his spine is crooked, so that it looks like two spines. This is what Rabbi Ḥananya [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the mishna reads Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus] meant: anyone with two backs and two spines has a blemish; but not literally two spines.
gershom:b24.1: His nose is sunken: between his eyes.
gershom:b25.1: Soled: the tip of his nose is drawn up.
gershom:b26.1: Bolem: his nostrils are stopped up.
gershom:b27.1: They said to him: you have gone too far: that is, you have departed from the words of the Sages; for the Rabbis hold that even if it is not so sunken that he can paint both of his eyes as one, but sunken less, it is a blemish. And [the eyes may] stand in their proper order, yet he sees with both of them in one place. [This last line seems to look ahead to the mishna’s case of one who sees the room and the upper story as one, discussed on 44a.]
